title: SynchronizationContext and ConfigureAwait
summary: Where a continuation runs, the classic UI deadlock, why ASP.NET Core has no context, and when ConfigureAwait(false) still matters.

steps.title: Where does the code after await run?
body: When `await` has to wait, it captures the **current context** and later asks it to run the continuation:
- If `SynchronizationContext.Current` is set, the continuation is **posted** to it. WPF, WinForms and MAUI install one that runs
everything on the **UI thread**, which is why you can touch controls after an `await` in a click handler. Classic ASP.NET
(System.Web, .NET Framework) had one per request.
- Otherwise, if the code runs on a custom `TaskScheduler`, it goes there.
- Otherwise it runs on a **thread-pool thread**.
**ASP.NET Core has no SynchronizationContext**, and neither do console apps or worker services. In them, continuations simply run on
the pool, and the context question disappears. In a UI app, or in a library that a UI app might call, it is very much alive.
`await task.ConfigureAwait(false)` says: *do not capture the context; continue on the pool*. .NET 8 added
`ConfigureAwait(ConfigureAwaitOptions)` for `Task` with `None`, `ContinueOnCapturedContext`, `SuppressThrowing` and `ForceYielding`.

steps.prompt: This runs as a console app. What does it print?
steps.explain: Console apps (like ASP.NET Core and worker services) have no SynchronizationContext. After the await, the code continues on a pool thread.

steps.title: The deadlock everyone hits once
body: A WPF button handler calls a library synchronously:
```csharp fragment
void OnSave(object s, RoutedEventArgs e)
var id = repo.SaveAsync(doc).Result;   // blocks the UI thread
// in the library
public async Task<int> SaveAsync(Doc d)
await http.PostAsJsonAsync("/docs", d);   // captures the UI context
return 42;                                 // wants to run on the UI thread
1. The UI thread blocks in `.Result`, waiting for `SaveAsync`.
2. The HTTP call finishes; the continuation is **posted to the UI thread**.
3. The UI thread is blocked waiting for that very continuation. Nothing moves. The window freezes forever.
The real fix is **async all the way**: `async void OnSave` with `await repo.SaveAsync(doc)`. The defensive fix, for library authors,
is `ConfigureAwait(false)` on **every** await in the library, so its continuations never need the caller's thread.

items: Inside a NuGet library that any kind of app may call
In an ASP.NET Core controller action
In a WPF click handler that sets `label.Content` after the await
In a shared SDK client used by a WinForms app and a web API
explain: Library code does not know who calls it, so it should not depend on (or block) the caller's context. App code in ASP.NET Core and
console apps has no context, so it changes nothing there (many teams leave it out for readability). UI code that touches controls
after the await *needs* the context: `ConfigureAwait(false)` there makes it crash with a cross-thread exception.

steps.prompt: A library method has two awaits. The first awaits a value from an in-memory cache that is usually already complete. Only the second one has `ConfigureAwait(false)`. Is that enough to avoid the UI deadlock?
options: Yes: the first await usually completes synchronously, so it stays on the UI thread, and the second one does not capture it
No: every await must have it, because whichever await first really waits must not capture the context
No: `ConfigureAwait(false)` only works on the first await
Yes, but only in .NET 8 and later
explain: The trap: `ConfigureAwait(false)` on an **already completed** task changes nothing (the fast path never leaves the thread). So the
code after a completed first await is still on the UI thread, with the context. If the *first* await that really waits lacks
`ConfigureAwait(false)`, it captures the UI context and deadlocks. On a cache miss that is the first one here. The rule is simple and
safe: in library code, put it on every await.

steps.title: Senior's toolkit: async correctness
steps.body: Analyzers find most async mistakes at build time; these find the rest at run time.

toolkit.what: Fail the build on an unawaited call (CS4014), a misused ValueTask (CA2012), and a blocking call inside an async method (CA1849).
flags: turn just these warnings into errors
toolkit.when: in CI; CA2007 (missing ConfigureAwait) only for library projects

toolkit.what: The VSTHRD rules: VSTHRD002 synchronous waits, VSTHRD100 async void, VSTHRD110 unobserved results, VSTHRD200 Async suffix.
toolkit.when: any codebase with a lot of async code

toolkit.what: Lists async state machines in a dump and the chain of what each one is awaiting: the async equivalent of a call stack.
toolkit.when: requests hang and the thread stacks show nothing (awaiting code is on no thread)

toolkit.cmd: Visual Studio: Debug > Windows > Parallel Stacks (Tasks view)
toolkit.what: Draws threads, or async tasks, as merged call graphs; works on a live process or a dump.
flags: switch between thread stacks and logical async stacks
toolkit.example: Open the .dmp in Visual Studio, Debug with Managed Only, then Parallel Stacks
toolkit.when: hundreds of threads or tasks that look alike

pairs: a call to an async method whose task is never awaited
a ValueTask awaited twice, or stored and misused
a blocking call (like `.Result` or `Thread.Sleep`) inside an async method

steps.title: Make the library safe to call from a UI thread
prompt: `ReportClient.FetchAsync` is a library method. A desktop app calls it from its UI thread with `.Wait()` (we cannot change the app this
Fix the **library** so that its continuations never need the caller's context. Keep the signature and the result
The tests call `FetchAsync` from a thread that has a UI-like `SynchronizationContext` and then block it with `.Wait(2000)`, exactly like
the app. In the tests, `GetTitleAsync` answers from a cache (already complete) and `CountRowsAsync` really waits.
starter: public static async Task<string> FetchAsync(Source source)
solution: public static async Task<string> FetchAsync(Source source)
template: dojoFinished = t.Wait(2000);   // the app blocks its UI thread, as in the bug report
Dojo.Check("FetchAsync completes while the calling UI thread is blocked", dojoFinished,
"It deadlocked: a continuation was posted to the blocked UI thread. Which await captured the context?");
Dojo.Eq("FetchAsync returns the report line", "Sales: 12 rows", dojoResult);
/// A context like WPF's: posted work runs only when the UI thread pumps messages. This one never pumps, because the thread is blocked.
public override void Post(SendOrPostCallback d, object? state) { /* queued for the UI thread, which is blocked */ }
public Task<string> GetTitleAsync() => Task.FromResult("Sales");   // cache hit: already complete
public async Task<int> CountRowsAsync() { await Task.Delay(20).ConfigureAwait(false); return 12; }

require.message: Every await in the library has ConfigureAwait(false) (a cache miss makes the first one wait too)

hints: The deadlock comes from an await that captures the context and then really waits. Which await waits here?
Add `.ConfigureAwait(false)` to **every** await in the library method, including the one on the cache, whose task is already complete.
explain: With the fix on only the first await, the test still deadlocks: that task is already complete, so the code continues on the UI thread
and the second await captures the context. That is why the rule for library code is *every* await, not the first one.
